Vorwerk — Friedrich Vorwerk (1893–1969), journalist and publisher. Schmitt had known him since Vorwerk’s time as an editor of the journal Der Ring. See Schmittiana III (1991), pp. 159–162, and Tb 1930–34 (index).
Beste — Theodor Beste (1894–1973), born in Neheim-Hüsten. From 1939 onward, as professor of business administration, he was Schmitt’s colleague at the Friedrich Wilhelm University in Berlin.
Welzel’s book — Hans Welzel, Vom irrenden Gewissen. Eine rechtsphilosophische Studie (Recht und Staat in Geschichte und Gegenwart, 145), Tübingen 1949.

The passage about the judge of heretics, for which Welzel gives no source, can be found in I. Kant, Die Religion innerhalb der Grenzen der bloßen Vernunft, in Werke in zehn Bänden, ed. W. Weischedel, Darmstadt 1975, vol. 7, pp. 860 ff.
Brecht’s Threepenny Novel, Munich 1946? — Not 1946, but 1949.
“Brute force has had its day …” — B. Brecht, Dreigroschenroman, in Gesammelte Werke, vol. 13, Frankfurt am Main 1967, pp. 999–1000.
Reading Ponceau — See above, note to p. 212.
Found a note from 24 August 1915 — See Tb 1915, p. 116.
And if it still has honor, it comes from me — Friedrich Hölderlin, The Death of Empedocles, Act 1, Scene 3:
The world is mine, and subject to me, serving me; all its powers are mine. Nature, which needs a master, has become my maid. And if it still has honor, it comes from me.

Just don’t write to this Dr. Lewald — Walter Lewald (1887–1986), jurist and co-editor of the Neue Juristische Wochenschrift, wrote in 1950 that Schmitt was a Luciferian spirit “who went astray into the worship of power and completed his work by deifying the Antichrist.” W. Lewald, “Carl Schmitt redivivus,” in Neue Juristische Wochenschrift 3 (1950), p. 377.
Non decet scribere ei qui vult proscribere — See above, note to p. 192. Here altered to mean: “It is not fitting to write to someone who wants to outlaw you.”
Hölderlin’s ode to Vanini — A counterpart to the ode “Empedokles,” stanza 3:
But sacred Nature, whom you loved while alive, who received you as you died, does not forget the deeds of men, and your enemies returned, like you, into the ancient peace.
Lucilio Vanini (1585–1619), philosopher and theologian, taught a pantheistic religion of nature and was tortured and burned at the stake in Toulouse in 1619.

Letter from Álvaro d’Ors to Father Welty — Among Schmitt’s papers is a letter from Álvaro d’Ors dated 7 May 1950 to Father Eberhard Welty, who had invited him to give a lecture on Vitoria at Walberberg; RW 265 no. 10717.

making a tactless rogue like Erich Kaufmann the guiding spirit of international law — The constitutional and international lawyer Erich Kaufmann (1880–1972), with whom Schmitt initially had a very friendly relationship when they were colleagues in Bonn, became a bitter enemy around 1927.

On 6 April 1927 Schmitt first recorded a negative judgment of Kaufmann in his diary: “heard the unbelievable gossip and slander Kaufmann has been spreading about me in Berlin.” Publication forthcoming.

From 1950 onward Kaufmann served as an adviser to the Federal Chancellery and the Foreign Office. See Helmut Quaritsch, “Eine sonderbare Beziehung. Carl Schmitt und Erich Kaufmann,” in Bürgersinn und staatliche Macht in Antike und Gegenwart. Festschrift für Wolfgang Schuller, Konstanz 2000, pp. 71–87.

To Tüngel — Richard Tüngel (1893–1970), co-founder and editor-in-chief of the weekly newspaper Die Zeit. Because he gave Schmitt a platform there, he was dismissed in 1955 at the urging of Countess Dönhoff.

Tüngel’s article in Die Zeit of 25 May 1950 was entitled “Neues Biedermeier Bonner Staatsschutz” and criticized efforts by the federal cabinet to create new categories of political crime such as “betrayal of the peace.”

Schmitt’s letter to Tüngel survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 13580. It is published in K. Burkhardt, ed., Carl Schmitt und die Öffentlichkeit. Briefwechsel mit Journalisten, Publizisten und Verlegern aus den Jahren 1923 bis 1983, Berlin 2013, pp. 87–88.
“Private property alienates …” — Karl Marx, Die deutsche Ideologie, in Karl Marx/Friedrich Engels, Werke, vol. 3, Berlin 1969, p. 212.

Count Spee’s Cautio Criminalis of 1631 — Schmitt is referring to the following edition: Cautio criminalis oder Rechtliches Bedenken wegen der Hexenprozesse, German edition by Joachim-Friedrich Ritter (Forschungen zur Geschichte des deutschen Strafrechts, 1), Weimar 1939. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 27068.
Mortisque peribunt / Argumenta tuae — See above, note to p. 219.
Gide: “c’était mettre le point d’honneur …” — See André Gide, Journal 1939–1949, Paris 1950, p. 44.

When one reads in André Gide that Hitler arose from Versailles — “Il n’y aurait jamais eu de Hitler sans le traité de Versailles.” — “There would never have been a Hitler without the Treaty of Versailles.” Gide, Journal, op. cit., p. 225.
the argumentum ad canem — Hegel wrote against Schleiermacher’s definition of religion as a feeling of “absolute dependence”:

“If religion in man is based only on a feeling, then this feeling can properly have no further determination than the feeling of his dependence. In that case the dog would be the best Christian, because he possesses this feeling most strongly and lives above all in this feeling. The dog even has feelings of redemption when his hunger is satisfied with a bone.”
Schleiermacher wrote to Karl Heinrich Sack on 28 December 1822:

“But what do you say to Herr Hegel, who in his preface to Hinrichs’s philosophy of religion attributes to me the view that because of absolute dependence the dog is the best Christian, and accuses me of animal ignorance about God? Things like that must simply be passed over in silence.”
Quoted in F. Schleiermacher, Kritische Gesamtausgabe. Schriften und Entwürfe, vol. 7: Der christliche Glaube 1821–1822, part 1, Berlin/New York 1980, p. LVII. See also Tb 1930–34, p. 450, note 2059.
With difficulty and complications … — Schmitt obtained the book through Peter Scheibert, who was traveling in the United States. See Schmitt to N. Sombart, 13 July 1950:
“What Peter Scheibert has brought me from the USA so far—for example Ernst Bloch’s Freiheit und Ordnung—has been disappointing.”
“C’est l’antisémite qui crée le juif” — “It is the antisemite who creates the Jew.” A. Gide, Journal, op. cit., p. 288.
“Les juifs sont les plus doux des hommes.” — “The Jews are the gentlest of men.” Ibid., p. 289.
Il est si doux — “He is so gentle.” See BW EJ, p. 154.

Control Council Law No. 10 — The law enacted by the Allies on 20 December 1945 formed the legal basis for trials concerning war crimes, crimes against peace, and crimes against humanity. It was not incorporated into the law of the Federal Republic because of concerns about the prohibition on retroactive criminal laws.
How proudly I wrote back then: Welcome, good and evil! — From the end of the preface to PuB, dated 20 August 1939.
Again and again I fell for the deception; again and again I escaped it. — Schmitt quoting himself: ECS, p. 88.

Only someone who knows his prey better than it knows itself can conquer it. — “The conquest of the disintegrated mass, its violent subjugation and reshaping by the army, is impossible—the army in its old organization no longer has the power to conquer, and the aristocracy of its commanders is no longer a historical force advancing into the future. For only someone who knows his prey better than it knows itself can conquer it, by subjugating it through his superiority in education and knowledge.”
Bruno Bauer, Die bürgerliche Revolution in Deutschland seit dem Anfang der deutsch-katholischen Bewegung bis zur Gegenwart, Berlin 1849, pp. 294–295.
Schmitt quoted this passage from Bruno Bauer frequently, and not only—as is sometimes claimed—after the defeat of 1945. See, for example, PuB, p. 333.
Monsieur Quine … — In Bernanos’s final novel, Monsieur Quine, the title character speaks on his deathbed of his “hunger for souls”:

“I took care not to change them. I revealed their own selves to them, with as much care as an entomologist needs to unfold the wings of a butterfly emerging from its chrysalis. Their Creator did not know them better than I did, and even through love one cannot possess anything as completely as I possessed those souls through this infallible act of possession, which does not wound the patient, leaves him undestroyed, and yet delivers him entirely into our hands, captured with all his most delicate shades, his iridescence, the whole color of life.”
Georges Bernanos, Monsieur Quine; here quoted from the German edition Die tote Gemeinde, Olten 1949, p. 284.
The time is coming, Nietzsche said … — See Friedrich Nietzsche, Werke in drei Bänden, ed. Karl Schlechta, 8th ed., Munich 1977, vol. 2, p. 672.
Heidegger, Holzwege, p. 205 — Schmitt quotes from Martin Heidegger, Holzwege, Frankfurt am Main 1950.
Lake Success — Village in the United States that served as the headquarters of the United Nations from 1946 to 1951.
Nietzsche: “With firm shoulders …” — F. Nietzsche, Werke, ed. Giorgio Colli and Mazzino Montinari, Munich 1999, vol. 10, p. 207.
Nietzsche: “Look at the world …” — Correctly: “Look at the world as though time had passed away: then everything crooked will become straight for you.” Ibid., p. 216.
Quid igitur lex? Propter transgressiones posita est — Vulgate, Galatians 3:19. “Why, then, the law? It was added because of transgressions.”
Τί οὖν ὁ νόμος; τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν προσετέθη — The same passage, Galatians 3:19, in the Greek New Testament.
Pros-etethe, that is, ex post? — προσετέθη means “was added.” The preposition πρός is primarily spatial in meaning but can also have a temporal sense.
for example in the Schott — In the Catholic missal known as the “Schott,” Galatians 3:19 reads: “Why, then, the law? It was established afterward because of transgressions.”
Anselm Schott, Das Meßbuch der heiligen Kirche lateinisch und deutsch, mit liturgischen Erklärungen und kurzen Lebensbeschreibungen der Heiligen, 36th ed., Freiburg im Breisgau 1932, p. 588.

The jurisprudence I speak of at the end of “The Plight of European Jurisprudence” — “European jurisprudence does not have to die together with the myths of law and the lawgiver. Let us recall once again the history of our suffering, for our strength is rooted in our trust in suffering. Then the genius will not abandon us, and it will become clear that even the confusion of languages can be better than Babylonian unity.”
C. Schmitt, Die Lage der europäischen Rechtswissenschaft, Tübingen 1949, p. 32.
Rome n’est plus dans Rome, elle est toute où je suis. — “Rome is no longer in Rome; Rome is wherever I am.” Pierre Corneille, Sertorius, Act 3, Scene 1.
Jürgen Rausch on Ernst Jünger — J. Rausch, “Ernst Jüngers Optik,” in Merkur 4 (1950), pp. 1069–1085; also published separately, Stuttgart 1951.
the three righteous comb-makers — See above, note to p. 41.
and if we killed them all, we would all have to take their place — Schmitt quotes Bruno Bauer inaccurately. Bauer actually writes:

“Luther once said in his table talk: ‘If all the useless people had to die, then we ourselves would have to become useless; for the devil must have useless grounds. So let them go on living, since God allows them to live.’ Thus the lord of this world needs the Jews in order to carry out his finite and worldly purposes, and his need is so great that he is already recruiting part of his army from among the Christians as well. But if there were no Jews, then all of us would have to take their place.”
B. Bauer, Das Judenthum in der Fremde, Berlin 1863, p. 77. See also BW EJ, p. 190.
A. Mitscherlich (Der Monat, issue 25, Oct. 1950) — Alexander Mitscherlich, “Ödipus und Kaspar Hauser. Tiefenpsychologische Probleme in der Gegenwart,” in Der Monat 2 (1950), pp. 11–18.
Verlaine’s Kaspar Hauser poem — “Gaspard Hauser chante” (1873/81); translated by Richard Dehmel as “Lied Kaspar Hausers” (1891) and by Stefan George as “Kaspar Hauser singt” (1915).
Analyze that phonetically for once! — Schmitt is probably thinking of Ernst Jünger, “Lob der Vokale,” in Sämtliche Werke, vol. 12, Stuttgart 1979, pp. 40 ff.
Compare Jünger’s address for Schmitt’s ninetieth birthday:

“…I once made a note, on the occasion of one of the unpleasant incidents that befell you in your capacity as a professor of constitutional law: ‘Those are simply the misfortunes of the profession.’ You heard about this and remarked: ‘To understand that, one has to know the significance the vowel I has for Ernst Jünger.’”
Carl Schmitt und Plettenberg. Der 90. Geburtstag (Plettenberger Miniaturen, 1), Plettenberg 2008, p. 17.
To Frau Jünger — See BW GJ, pp. 145–146.
Consolation is an absurd word — A line by Goethe that Schmitt occasionally quoted:
Yes, go on scolding, go on cursing; nothing better will ever come of it. For consolation is an absurd word: a man who cannot despair has no need to live.
